question: Did Jesus even exist? Isn't the evidence outside the Bible too thin to be sure?

ledger.heading: Fourteenth run (2026-11-20): an independent editor's read of the science area, and the area "The historical Jesus and the resurrection"

shortAnswer: He almost certainly existed, and the case doesn't depend on believing the Gospels are inspired. Paul, writing in the 50s, says he stayed with Peter and met James, "the Lord's brother." Josephus, a Jewish historian who never became a Christian, names "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ" in a passage most historians accept as his. Tacitus, a Roman with no sympathy for the movement, records that Christus was executed under Pontius Pilate. The skeptic is right that no document from Jesus' lifetime names him, that Christian copyists expanded Josephus's longer passage, and that Christians have overstated the evidence. But the theory that he never lived has to explain away a brother, a named executioner and a movement that began within living memory, and specialists of very different convictions, believers and unbelievers alike, judge that it can't. Who he was is a further question, and history alone doesn't settle it.

sections.heading: The objection at its strongest
sections.body:
The idea that Jesus never lived is older than most people assume. French writers of the 1790s, Volney and Dupuis among them, proposed it; Bruno Bauer argued it in Germany in the middle of the nineteenth century; and in 1909 the philosopher Arthur Drews published *Die Christusmythe*, which drew a two-day public debate in Berlin's Zoological Garden on 31 January and 1 February 1910. Its most careful modern form is Richard Carrier's *On the Historicity of Jesus* (2014), published by an academic press in biblical studies.

Carrier begins where any historian should, with the earliest evidence. Paul's letters are older than the Gospels, and Paul says almost nothing about Jesus' teaching, his miracles or where he went. He speaks of knowing Christ by revelation and through the Scriptures. On Carrier's reading, the first Christians believed in a heavenly Jesus, known through visions and through Israel's Scriptures, and the Gospels, written decades later, set him in Galilee and Judea as a man of recent history. The outside witnesses don't rescue the case. Josephus's longer passage was rewritten by Christians. Tacitus wrote generations after the events, and his sentence about Christ is either a later Christian addition, as Carrier argued in a journal article the same year, or a repetition of what Christians said about themselves; either way it adds nothing independent. Carrier weighs the evidence with the rules of probability and concludes that a Jesus who began as a heavenly figure is the better explanation. He grants openly that the near-universal judgment of qualified experts is against him.

Put at its strongest, the objection asks two things. If Jesus was a man of recent history, why is the earliest witness so quiet about his life? And why did no one outside the movement notice him while he lived?

sections.heading: What is true in it
sections.body:
A good deal, and a Christian loses nothing by granting it. No document from Jesus' lifetime mentions him: no inscription, no coin, no letter, no record of his trial. He left no writings of his own. Every full account of his life that survives was written by people who believed God had raised him, and the earliest Gospel, Mark, is usually dated around 70, some forty years after the crucifixion. Paul really does say little about what Jesus did and taught. And the longer passage about Jesus in Josephus was expanded by Christian copyists; almost no specialist now defends it as Josephus wrote it.

Christians have argued badly here too. Some have said the evidence for Jesus is better than the evidence for Julius Caesar, a line that began as a comparison of manuscript copies and was garbled in the repeating; Caesar is attested by coins struck in his lifetime, by inscriptions and by his own writings. Others have said no serious person has ever doubted that Jesus lived, which the history above disproves. A skeptic who has heard those claims is right to listen warily to what follows.

sections.heading: The evidence
sections.body:
Start where Carrier starts, with Paul, because Paul turns out to be the strongest witness against the theory. His undisputed letters were written in the 50s, some twenty to twenty-five years after the crucifixion. In one of them he describes going up to Jerusalem three years after his conversion to stay fifteen days with Cephas, Peter's Aramaic name, and adds: "But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the Lord's brother" (Galatians 1:19, BSB). Elsewhere he mentions "the Lord's brothers" as a known group who traveled with their wives (1 Corinthians 9:5, BSB), and Mark names a James among Jesus' brothers (Mark 6:3). Carrier reads "the Lord's brother" as a way of naming a fellow believer, since Paul calls Christians brothers throughout his letters. But Paul uses the phrase to set James apart from the apostles he didn't see, and a name every Christian shared would set no one apart. Paul also says that Jesus was "born of a woman, born under the law" (Galatians 4:4, BSB), that he was "a descendant of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3, BSB), that he was betrayed on a particular night, and that he was crucified. A man who had stayed fifteen days with Peter and met Jesus' brother is a strange witness to a Jesus no one had met.

Then Josephus. He was a priest's son who commanded Jewish forces in Galilee in the revolt against Rome, went over to the Romans and settled in Rome, where he finished his *Antiquities of the Jews* in the 90s. He never became a Christian. Origen, writing in the third century, says plainly that Josephus did not believe in Jesus as the Christ (*Against Celsus* 1.47). In the twentieth book Josephus tells how the high priest Ananus, in the gap between two Roman governors around 62, convened the Sanhedrin and "brought before them the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others" and had them stoned (*Antiquities* 20.200, in William Whiston's translation). Most historians, including many with no Christian commitment, accept this passage as Josephus's own. It comes in passing, inside a story about a high priest abusing his office, and a Christian copyist would more likely have written "the Lord's brother," as Paul did.

The longer passage, in the eighteenth book, should be shown as it stands. In Whiston's translation it reads: "Now there was about this time Jesus, a wise man, if it be lawful to call him a man; for he was a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of such men as receive the truth with pleasure. He drew over to him both many of the Jews and many of the Gentiles. He was [the] Christ. And when Pilate, at the suggestion of the principal men amongst us, had condemned him to the cross, those that loved him at the first did not forsake him; for he appeared to them alive again the third day; as the divine prophets had foretold these and ten thousand other wonderful things concerning him. And the tribe of Christians, so named from him, are not extinct at this day" (*Antiquities* 18.63-64). The "principal men" are some leaders of Josephus's own people in Jerusalem, not the Jewish people, and even in this form of the passage it is Pilate who condemns and a Roman cross that kills; the Study Bible's note on Mark 15 frames the trial the same way, with some Jerusalem authorities taking part in handing Jesus over and the decision and the execution Roman. A Jew who didn't believe Jesus was the Christ could not have written "He was the Christ," or that he rose on the third day as the prophets foretold. So the passage as it stands is not what Josephus wrote, and the question is whether he wrote anything there at all. The view that every word is his is now largely abandoned, and some scholars think he wrote none of it. The view held by many specialists, John Meier among them, is that Josephus wrote a shorter, neutral notice of a wise man and worker of wonders whom Pilate condemned to the cross, and that copyists added the phrases of faith. A tenth-century Arabic chronicle by Agapius, the Melkite bishop of Hierapolis, gives a more guarded form of the passage, which Shlomo Pines published in 1971; whether it preserves an earlier text of Josephus is disputed. The argument here doesn't need the longer passage. The James passage stands on its own.

Then the Romans. Writing early in the second century about the fire that burned much of Rome in 64, Tacitus explains the name of the people Nero blamed for it: "Christus, from whom the name had its origin, suffered the extreme penalty during the reign of Tiberius at the hands of one of our procurators, Pontius Pilatus" (*Annals* 15.44, in the translation of Church and Brodribb). Carrier's suggestion that a Christian copyist added the sentence has no manuscript to support it: this part of the *Annals* survives in a single medieval manuscript, the source of every later copy, so the case rests on arguments from style and content. He may be right that Tacitus took the information from what Christians said. But then what Christians were saying, and what a Roman historian saw no reason to doubt, was that their founder had been executed by a named Roman governor in a named reign, an odd thing for a movement of visionaries to claim about a heavenly figure. Pilate himself is attested: a stone found at Caesarea in 1961 names him prefect of Judea. Around 112 Pliny, writing to the emperor Trajan from Bithynia, reported that Christians met before daylight on a fixed day and "addressed a form of prayer to Christ, as to a divinity" (*Letters* 10.96, in Melmoth's translation). That tells us about Christians, not about Jesus, and shouldn't be made to say more. Suetonius, in his life of Claudius, says the emperor banished the Jews of Rome, who were making disturbances "at the instigation of one Chrestus," and Acts mentions the same expulsion (Acts 18:2). Whether Chrestus is a garbled Christus is disputed, and nothing should rest on it.

Finally, the earliest pagan who attacked Christianity at length took Jesus to be real. Celsus, in the second century, called him illegitimate and a sorcerer, a man from a Jewish village whose mother spun for her living. As far as the surviving sources show, no ancient opponent said he never lived. They said he was a fraud, which is a different charge.

sections.heading: The argument, laid out
sections.intro: This is a historical argument, an inference to the best explanation, about whether there was a man behind the Christian story.
steps: Paul, writing within about twenty-five years of the crucifixion, says he stayed with Cephas and met James, "the Lord's brother," and speaks of Jesus as born of a woman, of David's line, betrayed and crucified.

Josephus, a Jew who didn't believe in him, names James as "the brother of Jesus, who was called Christ," and Tacitus, a Roman who despised the movement, places Christ's execution under Pilate in the reign of Tiberius.

The theory that there was no such man must read "the Lord's brother" as a name for any believer, set aside Josephus's James passage, and explain why a movement of visionaries gave a heavenly figure a recent, shameful and datable Roman death; each of these moves is possible, and each is strained.
sections.conclusion: So: that Jesus was a Jewish teacher who lived in the first century and was crucified under Pontius Pilate is the best explanation of the evidence, by a wide margin. The argument shows that he lived and died. It doesn't show who he was.
sections.after: The weight sits on the first step, because Paul is the earliest witness and the one the theory most needs to reinterpret. A reader can test it by reading Galatians 1 and 2 whole and asking whether "James, the Lord's brother" reads like a name for any believer.

sections.heading: The strongest reply, and an answer
sections.body:
The strongest reply is that a consensus is not an argument, and that the evidence named here would be thin by any standard: a phrase in Paul, one sentence in Josephus, a line in Tacitus. Weighed with probability theory, without assuming Jesus existed, Carrier argues, these traces are better explained as the growth of a myth than as the footprints of a man. Scholars have been wrong together before.

The first half of that should be granted. Agreement among experts is evidence of where the arguments have led, not a substitute for them, and the traces really are few. But they are few in the way the traces of almost everyone of Jesus' station are few. Josephus tells of another Jesus, the son of Ananias, a countryman who began crying woe against Jerusalem four years before the war, was beaten, brought before the governor Albinus and released as a madman. If Josephus hadn't told the story, no trace of him would survive, and no one doubts he lived. A crucified preacher from Galilee was not the kind of man whom inscriptions and coins remember. The question is whether the evidence that does exist fits a man, and here it fits too well to be accidental: a brother who led the Jerusalem church, a disciple whose house Paul stayed in, a Roman governor whose term historians can date. As for probability, a calculation is only as good as the numbers put into it, and the numbers in this case are judgments about how likely each piece of evidence would be on each theory. The method moves the disagreement to those judgments. It doesn't settle it, and on the judgment that matters most, what Paul meant by "the Lord's brother," the plain reading favors history.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
sections.body: How much of Josephus's longer passage is original is still argued, and so is the value of the Arabic version. Whether Suetonius's Chrestus is Christ is open. How much of Jesus' own teaching historians can recover with confidence is a larger and older argument. Albert Schweitzer, surveying the nineteenth-century lives of Jesus in 1906, warned that "each individual created Him in accordance with his own character" (in W. Montgomery's translation), and the warning still applies to believers and skeptics alike. And the historical question leaves the deepest one where it was. History can establish that Jesus lived and was crucified. Whether he was who he said he was, and whether God raised him, are questions the rest of this area takes up.

sections.heading: Where Christians differ
sections.body: Christians differ on how much weight to rest on the outside sources, on whether Josephus wrote a core of the longer passage, and on how far historical study can take a believer. Some build much on the historians' agreement; others hold that faith rests on the apostles' testimony in Scripture and treat the outside sources as confirmation only. What they confess together is not in doubt. The Apostles' Creed says that Jesus "suffered under Pontius Pilate," and so ties the faith to a man of a particular time and place. Christianity confesses that he is truly God and truly man, and the second half of that confession is exactly what the historians' evidence touches.

otherSide: Richard Carrier, *On the Historicity of Jesus* (2014), and his article "The Prospect of a Christian Interpolation in Tacitus, Annals 15.44," *Vigiliae Christianae* 68 (2014).
further: Bart D. Ehrman, *Did Jesus Exist?* (2012), by an agnostic scholar, against the theory.

claims.claim: The first Christians believed in a heavenly Jesus known through visions and Scripture; the Gospels later placed him in history
There was no historical man behind the Christ of the Gospels
